newsitem.title: INDIA: Congress party tussle keeps Indian PM guessing.
newsitem.headline: Congress party tussle keeps Indian PM guessing.

text.p: India's Congress party, shoring up Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's minority alliance, was in disarray on Saturday in a leadership tussle that could decide the fate of the country's fragile government, politicians said.

Former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao, the man who kept Congress outside the coalition but pledged his party's backing for the 13-party United Front alliance government, quit his last party post on Thursday.
Rao resigned as Congress president in September and was virtually dismissed on Thursday as the head of the Congress Parliamentary Party (CPP).
Now, Deve Gowda must watch who emerges as the dominant force in Congress to see if he can count on that person for support, party officials said.
"The successor to Rao (as CPP leader) will carry out the party's policy towards the government," a party official close to new Congress president Sitaram Kesri told Reuters.

"Because the Congress has the responsibility to steer the nation on the right course, the issue of the CPP leadership is of paramount importance to the party," the official said on condition of anonymity.

Other officials said Rao's declaration to party deputies on Friday that his resignation did not signal his political oblivion meant the guessing game over the party's future would continue, officials said.
"I do not consider my resignation as CPP leader a terminal point. I have a long way to go with you," Rao told Congress legislators in a farewell address.
Newspapers said Rao's remarks indicated he would not allow Kesri an easy passage to become the CPP leader, a post that could qualify him to stake a claim to Deve Gowda's job.
Kesri is regarded by colleagues and rivals as a shrewd tactician who could split Deve Gowda's alliance to win support for a Congress-led coalition government.
Kesri's other rivals for the CPP post include former Congress ministers Sharad Pawar and Rajesh Pilot, both known to favour Congress joining a United Front government under Deve Gowda's leadership.
The CPP leadership tussle prompted Kesri to delay a vote on the issue by 10 days until January 3, Congress officials said.
Rao quit as party leader in September after a judge upheld a summons ordering him to appear in court to face criminal conspiracy charges.

Kesri wants Congress, which controls at least 142 votes in the 545-member lower house, to flex its muscles, but it trails the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party, the biggest single party in the lower house of parliament with 161 votes.
Deve Gowda's coalition has some 190 votes but they are split among parties ranging from free traders to communists.
Strains have emerged within the coalition, especially over economic policy which is spearheaded by Finance Minister P. Chidambaram, whose liberal thrust riles the left.
